== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable for longitudinal attrition (cross-sectional household survey with no follow-up wave), though survey non-response and item missingness rates are completely unreported (Tables 1-2 reflect N = 80 in most rows and an anomalous N = 82 in one row).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Comparisons of basic urban service access between Lahore (Punjab) and Peshawar (KPK) are wholly unadjusted despite major compositional confounders noted in the text—such as Ganj Bazar in Peshawar being an inner-city settlement heavily populated by displaced Afghan refugees and IDPs versus Kotli Ghazi in Lahore being a peri-urban agricultural subdivision near the Lahore Ring Road—with no multivariable adjustment, matching, or stratification.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak: Although Section 1 and Section 4 narratively review Pakistan's 18th Constitutional Amendment, provincial Local Government Ordinances/Acts in Punjab (2001, 2013, 2019) and KPK, and the Katchi Abadis Act (1992/2012), legal/administrative exposure is never measured at the household or settlement level and is reduced in the empirical analysis to an unadjusted two-neighbourhood contrast.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Household service access, drainage experience, satisfaction, and local governance assessments rely entirely on unvalidated self-report survey items with undisclosed wording, and Tables 1-2 exhibit arithmetic and tabulation errors (e.g., Table 1 NGOs row reports 15/80 as 20.0% rather than 18.8%; Table 2 'Politicization of service delivery' sums to 82 respondents and 101.3% rather than N = 80).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Water and sanitation outcomes ('safe drinking water' 52%, 'community level sanitation and waste disposal' 42%, 'restrooms' 42%, post-rain drainage issues 60%) are measured only via undefined binary self-reports without WHO/UNICEF JMP definitions, physical inspection, or water-quality testing, and service-specific percentages are not disaggregated by city in tabular form.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern: No survey protocol or pre-analysis plan is cited; city-level service-access comparisons are reported only as aggregate ranges in the Conclusion (62.5-87.5% in Lahore vs. 22.5-65.0% in Peshawar) while Tables 1-2 pool both cities without disaggregation; and the five 'good practice' vignettes in Section 3 are selectively chosen as success stories without systematic selection criteria.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Purposive selection of only two low-income settlements (Kotli Ghazi in Lahore and Ganj Bazar in Peshawar) with no sampling frame, no household recruitment or randomization procedure, no response rate, no stated sample size in prose (N = 80 inferred only from Tables 1-2), and predominantly male household-head respondents excluding women's direct perspectives.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: While the chapter names the two surveyed settlements (Kotli Ghazi in Lahore and Ganj Bazar in Peshawar) and states why those neighbourhoods were purposively chosen, it defines no household or respondent inclusion/exclusion criteria, no sampling frame, no household selection method, no survey dates, and does not even state the sample size in the text (N = 80 overall is only inferable by summing row counts in Tables 1 and 2).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: Macro-level city demographics for Lahore and Peshawar are summarized from secondary census/consultant reports, and brief neighbourhood backgrounds are given for Kotli Ghazi and Ganj Bazar, but study subjects are described only in a cursory paragraph ('majority of the respondents were males, and so were the heads of the households', 'average age of 48', 'more than half are illiterate') without sample size N, city-specific sample counts, exact demographic distributions, income figures, or year of data collection.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: The governance/institutional exposure of interest—provincial and municipal decentralization regimes in Punjab versus KPK and informal low-income settlement status—is discussed only narratively at the provincial level and operationalized empirically as residence in one purposively chosen neighbourhood per city, with no household- or settlement-level measurement of legal tenure (e.g., Katchi Abadi regularization), municipal jurisdiction, or administrative service coverage.
domain_ratings.where_found: Sections 1.1-1.3 [PDF Pages 3-6]; Section 2 [PDF Page 7]; Section 4 [PDF Pages 14-16]

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Neither informal/slum settlement classification ('low income areas' / 'selected slums and squatter settlements') nor household socio-economic deprivation and health status ('at least 50% have an average health') was defined or measured using objective, standardized criteria, official registries, or validated instruments.

Although the authors note major contextual differences between the two sites—most notably that Ganj Bazar in Peshawar is a central-city settlement heavily populated by displaced Afghan refugees and IDPs whereas Kotli Ghazi in Lahore is a peri-urban agricultural subdivision along the Ring Road—they do not identify refugee/migrant composition, household income, tenure security, or settlement age/location as confounders when attributing city differences in service access to provincial governance structures.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1.4 [PDF Pages 6-7]; Section 2 & Section 2.1 [PDF Pages 7-8]; Section 5 [PDF Pages 16-17]

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No design-based or statistical strategies (such as matching, stratification, or multivariable regression controlling for household socio-economic or migrant status) were stated or implemented to address confounding between the two surveyed settlements.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Outcomes—including access to 'safe drinking water', 'community level sanitation and waste disposal', 'restrooms', post-rain drainage problems, organizational satisfaction, and governance ratings—were measured solely through unvalidated household self-reports without questionnaire wording, operational thresholds (such as JMP definitions), or physical verification. In addition, Tables 1 and 2 contain internal count and percentage errors (e.g., Table 1 NGOs row lists 15/80 as 20.0% instead of 18.8%; Table 2 'Politicization of service delivery' sums to 82 respondents and 101.3% whereas all other rows sum to 80).

Despite stating in the Abstract that 'statistical analysis of access to basic services and satisfaction level was comprehensively gauged to link it with the prevailing governance structure', the paper reports only univariate/descriptive percentages on N = 80 respondents without confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, measures of association, or multivariable models, alongside arithmetic errors in Tables 1 and 2.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract [PDF Page 1]; Sections 2.1-2.5 & Tables 1-2 [PDF Pages 7-10]; Section 5 [PDF Page 16]

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: High methodological concern (all 8 JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional items rated 'No'). S1089 combines a narrative institutional overview of decentralization in Pakistan (18th Constitutional Amendment, Punjab and KPK Local Government Acts, Katchi Abadis Act) and five brief secondary 'good practice' vignettes with primary empirical data from a cross-sectional household survey conducted by the Urban Unit in two low-income settlements: Kotli Ghazi in Lahore (Punjab) and Ganj Bazar in Peshawar (KPK). Methodological reporting and internal validity are severely limited. The chapter omits survey dates, sampling frames, household recruitment criteria, response rates, questionnaire wording, and even the sample size in prose (total N = 80 is only deducible from row sums in Tables 1 and 2, where one row anomalously sums to 82 and several percentages are miscalculated). Respondents were predominantly male household heads, limiting representativeness for marginalized women discussed in the chapter. Water and sanitation outcomes ('safe drinking water' 52%, 'community level sanitation and waste disposal' 42%, 'restrooms' 42%) rely on undefined subjective self-reports, and the cross-province comparison attributing higher service access in Lahore (62.5-87.5%) than Peshawar (22.5-65.0%) to local governance arrangements is completely unadjusted for glaring neighbourhood-level confounders such as refugee/IDP concentration and peri-urban versus inner-city settlement structure.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Cross-sectional household survey in two purposively selected low-income urban settlements (Kotli Ghazi in Lahore, Punjab; Ganj Bazar in Peshawar, KPK; inferred total N = 80), embedded within a book chapter providing narrative legal/institutional mapping of decentralization and five secondary descriptive 'good practice' vignettes.
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract [PDF Page 1]; Section 1 National and City Context (1.1 Decentralization Policy, 1.2 Functional Gaps, 1.3 Institutional Mapping of Punjab and KPK, 1.4 Service Deficit in Lahore and Peshawar) [PDF Pages 2-7]; Section 2 Analysis of Access to Urban Services Based on the Household Survey & Tables 1-2 [PDF Pages 7-10]; Section 3 Good Practices and Innovations [PDF Pages 11-14]; Section 4 Understanding Barriers to Political and Social Inclusion [PDF Pages 14-16]; Section 5 Conclusion [PDF Pages 16-17].
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The chapter's sole primary empirical data collection is a quantitative cross-sectional household survey in two low-income settlements across Punjab and KPK designed to measure urban service access and governance satisfaction and link them to prevailing provincial/local governance structures (Abstract, PDF p. 1; Sect. 2, PDF pp. 7-10; Sect. 5, PDF p. 16). There is no longitudinal follow-up or quasi-experimental intervention/policy Shock design (ruling out ROBINS-I and JBI Cohort), and no primary qualitative data collection such as interviews, focus groups, or ethnography—the five 'good practice' cases in Section 3 are brief secondary vignettes 'quoted for their originality and innovation' rather than primary qualitative fieldwork (ruling out MMAT and CASP). Because the primary empirical component fits a conventional cross-sectional survey design, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the appropriate instrument rather than the fallback Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework.
